kurals.tamil:
மனைவிழைவார் மாண்பயன் எய்தார் வினைவிழைவார்
வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaivizhaivaar maanpayan eydhaar vinaivizhaivaar
ventaap porulum adhu.
kurals.meaning: Those who give themselves over to doting on their wives miss life's highest fruit; and that very indulgence is what people intent on real accomplishment choose to avoid.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a team captain who stops practising because he only wants to hang out at home all day. He may be comfortable, but the team never wins. People who want to do big things keep their comfort in balance with their work.
kurals.university: The chapter title penvazhich seral (பெண்வழிச் சேறல்) literally means 'going by a woman's way', and Parimelazhagar frames the whole chapter as advice to a ruler or man of affairs within the Porul (polity) section, placed among other vices to be avoided (chapters 92-94 on wanton women, drink and gambling). In this opening couplet manai-vizhaivaar (மனைவிழைவார், those who crave the wife or household pleasure) fail to reach maan-payan (மாண்பயன், the excellent fruit), which Parimelazhagar glosses as aram (virtue), while vinai-vizhaivaar (வினைவிழைவார், those who desire action) reject such indulgence as a hindrance to porul (wealth-making). Textual note: ytamizh and thirukkural.net read the third word as vinaivizhaiyaar (வினைவிழையார், 'those who do not desire action'), while thirukkural.com, kuraltheni.com and Parimelazhagar's own gloss read vinaivizhaivaar; we follow the latter. Also note that thirukkural.com wrongly prints Kalaignar's gloss for Kural 801 under this verse. Modern critics point out that the chapter assumes a male, elite reader and a patriarchal household; many contemporary readers (including Mu. Varadarasanar's 'considering domestic comfort paramount') take its target to be infatuation and neglect of duty rather than women as such, a reading supported by Valluvar's high praise of the wife in chapter 6 (வாழ்க்கைத் துணைநலம்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces how fixing the mind on pleasing objects grows into attachment and craving that cloud judgment.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's doting husband is a case of this chain: absorption in domestic pleasure crowds out the higher aim.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verse on attachment in general; it does not speak of wives or domestic life specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife.”
christianity.explanation: Paul observes that marriage naturally turns a man's attention toward pleasing his spouse and worldly concerns, as against undivided devotion to God.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it notes that preoccupation with pleasing a wife can draw energy away from a higher calling, though Paul does not condemn marriage.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close thematic parallel; Paul's frame is spiritual devotion rather than worldly achievement, and he applies the same point to wives in 7:34.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allāh. And whoever does that - then those are the losers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that even legitimate attachments to family and property can distract from the highest purpose.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that domestic attachment can cost a person the 'excellent fruit' of life.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified wording; the verse names wealth and children, not spouses, so the match is to the general principle of distraction.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Torah exempts a newly married man from military service and public duties for one year so that he may stay home and bring joy to his wife.
judaism.explanation: Jewish law sanctifies a period of devoted attention to a new spouse, but bounds it in time before public obligations resume.
judaism.tie_back: This offers a counterpoint: devotion to a wife is honored, yet the Kural's concern is with such devotion swallowing a person's duties permanently.
judaism._accuracy_note: A partial and contrasting parallel; it endorses time-limited devotion rather than warning against it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That is not a strong fetter, the wise say, which is made of iron, wood or hemp. But the infatuation and longing for jewels and ornaments, children and wives — that, they say, is a far stronger fetter, which pulls one downward and, though seemingly loose, is hard to remove.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls infatuation with family and possessions a fetter stronger than any chain.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's doting husband is held by just such a 'loose but strong' fetter that keeps him from higher attainment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on infatuation as a hindrance, though the Buddhist goal is renunciation rather than worldly success.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus lingers a full year feasting in Circe's palace until his crew remind him of home and he resumes his journey.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero's comfortable stay with an enchantress delays his true task until his companions rouse him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, absorption in pleasure with a woman stalls the man of action until he recalls his purpose.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel of indulgence delaying duty; Circe is not a wife.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle analyzes akrasia, the condition of the person who knows what is best but is overcome by desire for pleasure and acts against it.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the incontinent person's reason is overpowered by appetite, so his choices fail his own better judgment.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's man who chooses domestic pleasure over his duties fits Aristotle's portrait of a will weakened by pleasure.
philosophy._accuracy_note: General philosophical parallel about pleasure overriding judgment; not specific to marriage.

kurals.tamil:
பேணாது பெண்விழைவான் ஆக்கம் பெரியதோர்
நாணாக நாணுத் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Penaadhu penvizhaivaan aakkam periyadhor
naanaaka naanuth tharum.
kurals.meaning: The prosperity of a man who neglects his own responsibilities and gives himself wholly to desire for his wife becomes a great public embarrassment and brings shame upon himself.
kurals.elementary: If a class president stops doing the job and just lets his best friend decide everything, the whole class feels let down, and he ends up embarrassed too. Holding a job means doing it yourself.
kurals.university: Penaadhu (பேணாது, 'without guarding/caring for') is read by Parimelazhagar as neglecting one's own aanmai (ஆண்மை, manliness, i.e. capacity for independent action), while pen-vizhaivaan (பெண்விழைவான்) is one who desires the 'femininity' of his wife. The aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity) he holds becomes a periyadhor naan (பெரியதோர் நாண், a great shame) first for men generally and then for himself; Parimelazhagar explains that because the wife effectively controls the giving and enjoyment of that wealth, the public sees the man's agency as transferred to her. Manakkudavar reads penaadhu as neglecting aram and porul (virtue and wealth). Kalaignar's modern gloss shifts the emphasis to a man who abandons his principles to chase a woman, illustrating the trend among twentieth-century commentators to recast the chapter as a critique of infatuation rather than of women's agency. The text is uniform across ytamizh, thirukkural.net, thirukkural.com and kuraltheni. Contemporary critics note that the verse's notion of 'shame to all men' reflects a gendered honour code of its era.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Dasharatha, bound by boons he had granted his beloved queen Kaikeyi, is compelled to exile his heir Rama, to the dismay of his court and people.
hinduism.explanation: A king's indulgence of a favoured queen leads him to act against his own judgment and his kingdom's welfare.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, the king's power becomes a source of grief and public dismay when it is steered by private attachment.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known parallel; the narrative also stresses truth to one's word and the role of the maid Manthara, so it is not purely about uxoriousness.

christianity.quote_or_event: King Lemuel records his mother's counsel not to give his strength to women nor his ways to that which destroys kings.
christianity.explanation: A queen mother advises her royal son that dissipated attachments ruin rulers.
christianity.tie_back: The same concern as the Kural's address to the ruler; notably, here the warning itself comes from a woman.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match for a ruler's dissipation; wording paraphrased because it could not be re-verified live.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beautified for people is the love of that which they desire - of women and sons, heaped-up sums of gold and silver, fine branded horses, and cattle and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of worldly life, but Allāh has with Him the best return.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an lists attractions of worldly life that people naturally love, while pointing to a higher return.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's man is captured by one such attraction to the point of neglecting his responsibilities.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified wording; it describes natural desires as temporary goods rather than as sources of shame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.”
judaism.explanation: The narrator of Kings attributes Solomon's decline to his attachment to his many foreign wives.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a powerful man's attachment to his wives leads to the loss of his integrity and standing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; the biblical concern is idolatry rather than worldly duty, and modern scholarship notes the narrative's polemical framing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web.”
buddhism.explanation: Infatuation traps a person in a web of his own making.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man is likewise caught in a predicament he spun himself, ending in shame.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; parallels self-made entrapment by desire but not public shame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hector rebukes his brother Paris, who prefers Helen's chamber to the battlefield, as a disgrace to his family and city.
greek_mythology.explanation: Paris's devotion to Helen while his people fight makes him an object of reproach even to his own brother.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's picture of a man whose attachment brings shame on himself and others.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close narrative parallel; Helen is not his wife by lawful marriage in the Greek view.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch portrays Mark Antony neglecting command and statecraft for Cleopatra, culminating in his flight after her at Actium.
philosophy.explanation: The moralist-biographer presents Antony as a capable man whose judgment was captured by passion.
philosophy.tie_back: Antony is a classical example of the Kural's warning that power steered by attachment ends in shame.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong moral parallel; modern historians regard Plutarch's portrait as shaped by Roman propaganda against Cleopatra.

kurals.tamil:
இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லாருள் நாணுத் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Illaalkan thaazhndha iyalpinmai egngnaandrum
nallaarul naanuth tharum.
kurals.meaning: The unnatural habit of cowering before one's wife will always make a man feel ashamed in the company of good people.
kurals.elementary: If you are always too scared to say what you think, even to someone you love, you may feel awkward around friends who speak up honestly. Love works best when both people can speak freely.
kurals.university: Iyalpinmai (இயல்பின்மை) means 'that which is not natural', and Parimelazhagar glosses the whole phrase as the fear (achcham) that makes a man stoop (thaazh) before his wife; within his patriarchal frame, it is 'unnatural' because he expects the wife to be the deferential one. He adds that when a husband is so cowed, no one guides the household and every fault follows, so he is ashamed among the nallaar (நல்லார், the good) at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). Manakkudavar reads it simply as the ruinous habit of stooping to the wife. Kalaignar narrows it to a husband who fails to correct a wife lacking good character, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses fear, showing modern commentators softening the verse toward a critique of timidity. The text is identical in all four sources consulted. Modern readers rightly note that the assumption that deference is natural only for wives is a historical norm, not a universal truth, while the verse's underlying point about a fear-driven partnership remains discussable.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa ends the Raghu dynasty's story with King Agnivarna, who abandons governance for pleasures in the inner palace and dies of his excesses, leaving a pregnant queen to rule.
hinduism.explanation: The epic poet presents the last king's absorption in the women's quarters as the ruin of a glorious line.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's shame before the good is mirrored in the disgrace of a king who neglected his realm for private pleasure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match for a ruler's indulgence; it concerns sensual excess rather than fear of a wife, and the poem gives the queen a dignified final role.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs says it is better to live in a corner of the housetop than to share a wide house with a quarrelsome woman.
christianity.explanation: Wisdom literature acknowledges the misery of a household dominated by strife.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural it recognizes an unhealthy domestic dynamic, though it advises distance rather than warning of shame.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak match; it concerns domestic strife, not a husband's timidity, and reflects gendered assumptions of its time.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive - then indeed, Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an cautions that family members can pull a believer away from what is right, while urging forgiveness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that yielding to a spouse against one's better judgment brings harm.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; the verse is gender-neutral ('spouses') and pairs caution with forgiveness, which the Kural lacks.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Queen Vashti refuses King Ahasuerus's summons, his counsellors fear that all wives will despise their husbands, and a decree is sent that every man should rule his own house.
judaism.explanation: The court treats one queen's independence as a threat to every husband's honour.
judaism.tie_back: The same anxiety about a husband's public standing drives the Kural; many readers find the Esther episode deliberately satirical of that anxiety.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close parallel on male honour and public shame; modern Jewish and feminist readings treat the scene as ironic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes seven kinds of wives to Anathapindika's daughter-in-law, from a 'murderous' wife to a 'mother-like', 'sister-like' or 'friend-like' wife, judging each by conduct.
buddhism.explanation: Rather than condemning deference either way, the Buddha evaluates marital relationships by kindness and good character.
buddhism.tie_back: This offers a counterpoint: the problem in the Kural is better understood as an unhealthy relationship than as any submission to a wife as such.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.59 (Bhariya Sutta; numbered 7.63 in some editions)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Indirect; it is addressed to a wife about her conduct and only loosely relates to a husband's timidity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Xenophon has Socrates explain that he lives with the famously difficult Xanthippe as a horseman trains on a spirited horse, to learn to deal with all people.
greek_mythology.explanation: Socrates treats patience with a strong-willed wife as training in self-mastery rather than as disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: what one tradition calls shameful submission another frames as composure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrasting rather than parallel, and from Socratic literature rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle criticizes Sparta, arguing that much of its affairs were managed by women and that this contributed to the state's love of wealth and decline.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle views women's influence over men in public life as a structural weakness of a polity.
philosophy.tie_back: This parallels the Kural's political frame, while modern scholars treat Aristotle's account as a product of his gender theory.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Real parallel in a political treatise; Aristotle's claims about Sparta are contested by historians.

kurals.tamil:
மனையாளை அஞ்சும் மறுமையி லாளன்
வினையாண்மை வீறெய்த லின்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaiyaalai anjum marumaiyi laalan
vinaiyaanmai veereydha lindru.
kurals.meaning: A man who lives in fear of his wife, and so forfeits the merit that leads to a good hereafter, will never win acclaim for his work, however capable he may be.
kurals.elementary: A painter who is too afraid of anyone's opinion to paint what he really sees will never make a great painting. Fear holds back good work.
kurals.university: Marumai-ilaalan (மறுமையிலாளன்) means 'one without (merit for) the next world'; Parimelazhagar explains that such a man cannot perform the duties of the householder (illaram) properly and so loses the reward of the hereafter. Vinai-aanmai (வினையாண்மை, the capacity to direct undertakings) may exist, but it will not attain veeru (வீறு, distinction, acclaim) among the good, because one who lacks his own nature cannot bring work to completion. Manakkudavar adds that this verse means such a man will not create wealth. Textual note: ytamizh, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com divide the line as 'வீறெய்த லின்று' while kuraltheni prints 'வீறெய்தல் இன்று'; this is a difference of word-spacing (சீர் division vs. word division), not wording. Kalaignar gives a distinctive modern reading, taking the man as one who fears to undertake married life at all, a reinterpretation that avoids the gendered fear. Contemporary critics observe that the verse links domestic authority to public efficacy in a way typical of premodern political ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Shantanu, smitten by Satyavati, accepts her father's condition that her sons inherit the throne, leading his heir Devavrata to renounce kingship and marriage forever as Bhishma.
hinduism.explanation: A king's infatuation leads him to a concession with far-reaching consequences for the dynasty.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural warns, a ruler's judgment bent by attachment compromises his work and legacy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Real narrative parallel; the condition came from Satyavati's father, not from fear of a wife.

christianity.quote_or_event: Pilate's wife sends him a message during Jesus' trial urging him to have nothing to do with that just man, but Pilate yields to the crowd instead.
christianity.explanation: Here the wife gives the righteous counsel and the husband's failure is in not heeding her.
christianity.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: in this story a man's worth would have been served by listening to his wife.
christianity._accuracy_note: Contrasting parallel, included to show that wifely counsel is not uniformly portrayed as harmful.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allāh has with Him a great reward.”
islam.explanation: Family and possessions are described as tests whose handling determines one's reward with God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly ties a man's handling of domestic life to his merit in the next world.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified; shares the link between domestic life and the hereafter but does not mention fear of a spouse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But there was none like unto Ahab, which did sell himself to work wickedness in the sight of the LORD, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.”
judaism.explanation: The book of Kings presents Ahab as a king whose deeds were driven by his wife's instigation.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's view that a ruler led by his wife forfeits a good name and a good hereafter.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; the text places responsibility on Ahab himself ('did sell himself'), and modern scholarship notes Jezebel's portrayal is polemical.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a person tormented by evil thoughts, who is passion-dominated and given to the pursuit of pleasure, his craving steadily grows. He makes the fetter strong, indeed.”
buddhism.explanation: Domination by passion strengthens the bonds that hold one back.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man, dominated within his household, similarly cannot achieve distinction.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; general teaching on passion, not about fear of a spouse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The seer Amphiaraus foresees his death in the war of the Seven against Thebes, but his wife Eriphyle, bribed with the necklace of Harmonia, compels him to go.
greek_mythology.explanation: Bound by an agreement to abide by his wife's decision, a wise man is forced into a doomed undertaking.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's man whose actions are governed by his wife cannot bring his work to a good end.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good mythic parallel; the myth places the moral fault squarely on Eriphyle's bribery.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus begins his handbook by distinguishing what is in our power from what is not, warning that one who fears what others control becomes a slave.
philosophy.explanation: Freedom, for the Stoic, lies in governing one's own judgments rather than being ruled by fear of others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's fearful husband lacks the inner freedom that the Stoics thought necessary for good action.
philosophy._accuracy_note: General principle about fear and freedom; not about marriage.

kurals.tamil:
இல்லாளை அஞ்சுவான் அஞ்சுமற் றெஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Illaalai anjuvaan anjumat regngnaandrum
nallaarkku nalla seyal.
kurals.meaning: A man who is afraid of his wife will always be afraid even to do good things for good people.
kurals.elementary: If you are scared to share your snack with a hungry classmate because someone might be cross with you, fear is stopping you from being kind. Kindness needs a little courage.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar glosses nallaar (நல்லார், the good) as gods, ascetics, the wise, one's two elders (parents) and worthy guests, and nalla seyal (நல்ல செயல்) as giving them what they need; even when the wealth is his own earning, the fearful husband hesitates. He supports the reading with a parallel from the Jain Tamil epic Civaka Cintamani (மண்மகள் 217): 'illaalai anji virunthin mugam kondra nenjin pullaalan', a man who, fearing his wife, turned away the face of a guest. Manakkudavar sums the verse as meaning such a man cannot practise aram (virtue). Kalaignar inverts the sense, reading that a man anxious not to err in doing good will heed a watchful wife, a strikingly egalitarian modern reinterpretation. The text is identical across the four sources. Critics note that the verse presumes hospitality and charity are the husband's prerogative, a presumption that modern readers can retain as a call to generosity without its gendered frame.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad's parting instruction to students includes treating mother, father, teacher and guest as divine.
hinduism.explanation: Honouring and serving guests and elders is part of the householder's sacred duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The 'good deeds to the good' that the fearful husband neglects are precisely these duties of hospitality and reverence.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the content of the neglected duty, not the cause (fear of a wife).

christianity.quote_or_event: Herod, who feared John the Baptist as a just and holy man, has him beheaded after a promise made at a banquet, at the request of Herodias through her daughter, though he was exceedingly sorry.
christianity.explanation: A ruler who respected a righteous man nonetheless harms him rather than lose face and displease his wife's faction.
christianity.tie_back: This is close to the Kural: fear of displeasing those at home overrides doing right by the good.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; Herod's oath and his guests' presence also drive the outcome.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an condemns Abu Lahab together with his wife, the 'carrier of firewood', for their joint hostility to the Prophet.
islam.explanation: A husband and wife are portrayed as reinforcing each other in opposing a righteous messenger.
islam.tie_back: Loosely parallels the Kural's concern that domestic influence can turn a man against the good.
islam._accuracy_note: Weak match; the surah holds both spouses equally responsible rather than describing a fearful husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, Job answers that she speaks foolishly, and he does not sin with his lips.
judaism.explanation: Job holds to integrity even against the counsel of his closest companion.
judaism.tie_back: Job is the opposite of the Kural's fearful husband: he will not let domestic pressure divert him from righteousness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Contrasting exemplar; rabbinic tradition also reads Job's wife sympathetically as speaking from grief.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vessantara Jataka, Prince Vessantara gives away everything in perfect generosity, and his wife Maddi supports and shares his gifts and exile.
buddhism.explanation: Husband and wife together embody unstinting generosity.
buddhism.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: a spouse can strengthen rather than inhibit good deeds to others.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrasting parallel; the tale also raises its own ethical questions about giving away one's family.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The aged couple Baucis and Philemon together welcome disguised gods into their humble home and are rewarded.
greek_mythology.explanation: A husband and wife share in generous hospitality toward strangers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This shows the alternative to the Kural's scenario: a marriage in which good deeds to the worthy are done jointly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrasting exemplar of joint hospitality; Roman literature of Greek myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes liberality as the virtue of giving the right amounts to the right people at the right time, with pleasure rather than pain.
philosophy.explanation: A generous person gives readily and gladly to worthy recipients.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's fearful husband lacks this readiness, giving to the good with fear rather than gladness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the virtue at stake, not the cause of its failure.

kurals.tamil:
இமையாரின் வாழினும் பாடிலரே இல்லாள்
அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Imaiyaarin vaazhinum paatilare illaal
amaiyaardhol anju pavar.
kurals.meaning: Even if they live as splendidly as the gods, men who are afraid of their wife's slender, bamboo-like arms have no real dignity.
kurals.elementary: A superhero with amazing powers is not much of a hero if he is too scared to act. What makes someone admirable is courage, not just strength or riches.
kurals.university: Imaiyaar (இமையார், 'the unblinking ones') is a classical Tamil epithet for the gods; paatu (பாடு) here means dignity or worth, and paatilar those lacking it. Amai-aar-thol (அமையார்தோள்) compares the wife's shoulders or arms to amai (bamboo), a conventional image of feminine grace; Parimelazhagar notes that the slender image heightens the irony: a warrior who conquered heroes' arms yet fears these gentle ones has no aanmai (manliness). He reads 'living like the gods' as the life of heroes who reached heaven through valour, and says this verse closes a group of four (903-906) on the fault of fearing the wife. Manakkudavar takes it to mean that even the wealthy are not respected by others. Kalaignar again reinterprets, aiming the criticism at men who submit to a wife merely for beauty, not for wisdom or character. The text is uniform across sources. Modern critics note the verse's equation of dignity with masculine dominance as a historically situated value.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Pururavas, after the apsara Urvashi leaves him, wanders distraught and pleads with her to return, while she counsels him to recover himself.
hinduism.explanation: A great king is reduced to helplessness by his attachment to a celestial woman.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's man who lives like the gods yet lacks dignity, Pururavas's royal splendour cannot hide his dependence.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel on dependence rather than fear; Urvashi is not presented as domineering.

christianity.quote_or_event: Samson, the strongest man in Israel, yields his secret to Delilah's persistent pleading and loses his strength and freedom.
christianity.explanation: Extraordinary power proves useless once a man cannot stand firm against the woman he loves.
christianity.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's point that even godlike strength is worthless when a man is governed by a woman's will.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel; Delilah is not Samson's wife and acts as an agent of his enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: When the governor's wife falsely accuses Joseph, her husband, though he sees the truth, merely tells Joseph to overlook the matter and asks his wife to seek forgiveness.
islam.explanation: A powerful official acknowledges wrongdoing at home but lacks the resolve to act on it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's dignified-seeming man who will not stand up within his own household finds a parallel in the governor's weak response.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial parallel based on the narrative; the Qur'an does not explicitly describe the governor as fearing his wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah in all that she says regarding Hagar and Ishmael.
judaism.explanation: Here divine instruction explicitly directs a patriarch to follow his wife's counsel.
judaism.tie_back: A counterpoint to the Kural: in Genesis, heeding one's wife can be the path God endorses.
judaism._accuracy_note: Contrasting text; rabbinic tradition cites it to show that wives' counsel can be prophetically sound.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha's half-brother Nanda, newly ordained, pines for the beauty he left at home, until the Buddha shows him a higher aim and he becomes an arahant.
buddhism.explanation: A prince-turned-monk is held back by longing for a woman until he redirects his aspiration.
buddhism.tie_back: As with the Kural's godlike man without dignity, Nanda's status means little until he masters his attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel on longing rather than fear; the woman is his betrothed, not his wife.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ares, the god of war, is caught in Hephaestus's net with Aphrodite and becomes a laughing stock before the assembled gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: The mightiest warrior-god is rendered ridiculous by his passion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's man living like the gods yet lacking dignity, Ares's divinity cannot save him from humiliation.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel on loss of dignity through passion; adultery rather than marital fear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch advises that a husband should govern his household not as a master over property but as the soul over the body, through sympathy and goodwill.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch's ideal marriage combines partnership and affection with the husband's responsible leadership.
philosophy.tie_back: This reflects the same ancient household ideal behind the Kural, while emphasising mutual goodwill rather than fear in either direction.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the premodern household ideal; section reference given from standard Moralia numbering and should be checked.

kurals.tamil:
பெண்ணேவல் செய்தொழுகும் ஆண்மையின் நாணுடைப்
பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Penneval seydhozhukum aanmaiyin naanutaip
penne perumai utaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The modest dignity of a woman is worthier than the so-called manhood of a man who lives only by running his wife's errands.
kurals.elementary: Being a grown-up does not mean being bossy, and it does not mean just following orders either. A person with self-respect, whoever they are, deserves more admiration than someone who has given up thinking for themselves.
kurals.university: Pen-eval (பெண்ணேவல்) is 'a woman's command', and the man who 'conducts himself doing it' (seydhu ozhugum) is contrasted with naanutaip penne (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே), the woman possessed of naan (நாண், modesty, sense of shame). Parimelazhagar notes that 'modest woman' is added deliberately as the opposite of the shameless man: the wife who issues commands is not the point of comparison, but rather womanhood marked by naan, which he regards as superior to such manhood. He also observes the emphatic separation of 'penne' at the line's start. Manakkudavar reads that such men are not respected by others. The verse is notable because, within its gendered frame, it affirms that a woman's perumai (பெருமை, greatness) can exceed a man's; modern feminist readers note, however, that it values women for modesty while denying men the role of following a woman. Text is identical across sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the forest exile, Draupadi rebukes Yudhishthira for his passivity after the dice game and urges him to reclaim his kingdom by righteous force.
hinduism.explanation: The epic gives a woman the voice of spirited dignity against a husband's resignation.
hinduism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's second half: a woman's dignity can surpass a man's, while complicating the first by showing a wife's counsel as valuable.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial and complicating parallel; the epic presents her counsel sympathetically.

christianity.quote_or_event: Barak refuses to go into battle unless the prophetess Deborah goes with him, and she tells him the honour will therefore go to a woman, as Jael later kills Sisera.
christianity.explanation: A commander's dependence on a woman means the glory of victory passes to women.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, a woman's dignity outshines that of a man who will not act on his own, though the text honours Deborah and Jael rather than shaming women's leadership.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel; the biblical narrative celebrates female leadership, which differs from the Kural's frame.

islam.quote_or_event: The Queen of Sheba consults her chiefs, who defer to her judgment, and she chooses a wise and peaceful course before submitting to God with Solomon.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an portrays a woman ruler as prudent and her counsellors as rightly deferring to her.
islam.tie_back: A counterpoint: following a woman's lead here is wise, and her dignity is affirmed.
islam._accuracy_note: Contrasting parallel about a woman's wise authority.

judaism.quote_or_event: Abigail, wife of the boorish Nabal, wisely intercedes with David and averts bloodshed, earning his praise for her discretion.
judaism.explanation: A wife's good judgment far exceeds her husband's, and the narrative honours her.
judaism.tie_back: This agrees with the Kural that a woman's dignity can surpass a man's, while showing a woman's initiative as praiseworthy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial parallel; Abigail acts without her husband's command rather than commanding him.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Therigatha preserves the verses of early Buddhist nuns who attained liberation, celebrating their insight and resolve.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism records women's spiritual accomplishment in their own voices.
buddhism.tie_back: It affirms, as the Kural's second line does, that a woman's greatness can be real and exemplary.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Thematic only; it does not address men following women's commands.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, as penance, serves Queen Omphale of Lydia, and later tradition depicts him spinning wool in women's dress while she wears his lion-skin and club.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest hero, performing a woman's commands, becomes a classical emblem of reversed roles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the closest mythic image of the Kural's 'manhood that does a woman's bidding'.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; the spinning-and-dress motif comes from later sources such as Ovid rather than Apollodorus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that women of the guardian class should receive the same education and share the same duties as men.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's Socrates holds that capacity, not sex, should determine one's role in the city.
philosophy.tie_back: A counterpoint: Plato's argument undercuts the assumption that a man following a woman is inherently shameful.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Contrasting philosophical position; Plato still holds women to be generally weaker.

kurals.tamil:
நட்டார் குறைமுடியார் நன்றாற்றார் நன்னுதலாள்
பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nattaar kuraimutiyaar nandraatraar nannudhalaal
pettaangu ozhuku pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who live only as their fair-browed wife wishes will neither meet the needs of their friends nor do any good deed.
kurals.elementary: If you only ever do what one person wants, you might forget to help your other friends when they need you. Good friends keep room in their life for everyone who counts on them.
kurals.university: Nattaar (நட்டார்) are those who have formed friendship (natpu), and kurai mudiyaar (குறைமுடியார்) means they will not fulfil their friends' needs; nandru aatraar (நன்றாற்றார்) means they will not perform good deeds, which Parimelazhagar specifies as aram that aids the next world. Nan-nudhalaal (நன்னுதலாள், 'she of the fair forehead') is a conventional epithet he compares with 'bamboo-like shoulders' in 906, and pettaangu (பெட்டாங்கு) means 'as she desires'. His reasoning is that the wife cannot herself command and give wealth for these purposes, so both this-worldly and other-worldly duties lapse. Fitting the chapter's place in the Natpiyal (friendship) section, the verse highlights obligations to friends. The text is uniform across sources; Sivayogi Sivakumar's playful gloss reading pettaangu as 'like a pottu (forehead mark)' is a modern pun, not the classical sense. Modern readers may take the general point that any single relationship which crowds out duties to friends and community is unhealthy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sugriva, restored to his throne with Rama's help, forgets his promise to search for Sita while enjoying pleasures with Tara and Ruma, until Lakshmana confronts him in anger.
hinduism.explanation: A king indulging in the women's quarters neglects a debt to the friend who helped him.
hinduism.tie_back: This is a near-exact illustration of the Kural: absorbed in pleasure, a man fails to meet his friend's need.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel; notably it is Tara who wisely calms Lakshmana, so the women are not simply the cause.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable of the great supper, invited guests offer excuses, one citing his new marriage, and the host fills his table with the poor instead.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, attachment to a wife becomes an excuse to neglect a higher call and a host's invitation.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; marriage is one of several excuses in the parable, which targets worldly preoccupation generally.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an warns believers that if fathers, sons, brothers, spouses, relatives, wealth, trade and homes are dearer to them than God, His Messenger and striving in His cause, they should await God's decision.
islam.explanation: Family attachments, including to spouses, must not outrank one's higher obligations.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns that devotion to a wife must not displace duties to friends and to virtue.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; matches the principle of ranking attachments, not friendship specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thy house be wide open, and let the poor be members of thy household. Engage not in too much conversation with women. They said this with regard to one’s own wife, how much more [does the rule apply] with regard to another man’s wife.”
judaism.explanation: Yose ben Yochanan pairs open-handed hospitality with a caution against excessive absorption in conversation with women, including one's wife.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts link a man's generosity to others with not letting domestic intimacy consume his attention.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; the latter clause is widely discussed today as reflecting rabbinic-era gender attitudes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In his advice to the young householder Sigala, the Buddha lists reciprocal duties of husband and wife and also the duties one owes to friends and companions, such as generosity and help in need.
buddhism.explanation: The ideal householder balances obligations to spouse with obligations to friends and to religious teachers.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's man fails exactly this balance, letting one relationship eclipse friendship and good works.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good parallel on balanced duties; notably it asks the husband to honour his wife and hand over household authority to her.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Mercury rebukes Aeneas for building Carthage for Dido while forgetting his destined kingdom and his people's future, and Aeneas departs.
greek_mythology.explanation: A leader absorbed in a queen's affairs neglects his obligations to his companions and his son.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, devotion to a beloved leads a man to fail those who depend on him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong parallel from Roman epic; Dido's tragedy also invites sympathy for her rather than blame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle holds that friendship is among the greatest external goods and that the good person must act for his friends' sake, even at cost to himself.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, a flourishing life requires active care for friends.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's man who neglects his friends' needs forfeits this essential good.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the neglected duty of friendship, not its cause.

kurals.tamil:
அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்
பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aravinaiyum aandra porulum piravinaiyum
peneval seyvaarkan il.
kurals.meaning: Virtuous deeds, well-earned wealth and even other pleasures are all absent from those who simply do whatever their wives command.
kurals.elementary: A good life has three parts: being kind, working hard, and having fun. If someone lets another person run every part of their life, they can end up missing all three.
kurals.university: This verse maps directly onto the three aims of the Kural itself: aram (அறம், virtue), porul (பொருள், wealth) and, as Parimelazhagar glosses pira-vinai (பிறவினை, 'other deeds'), inbam (இன்பம், pleasure). He explains that once virtue and wealth are gone, even pleasure is lost because its direction lies with the wife, and he notes that verses 907-909 together treat the fault of doing the wife's bidding (eval). Manakkudavar adds that even men without fear, if they simply obey, lose all three. Textual note: some editions print pen-eval as one word (பெண்ணேவல்), as in 907, while all four sources consulted print 'பெண்ஏவல்' here. Kalaignar narrows the target to men enslaved by arrogant women's orders, a reading that limits the claim. Contemporary scholars stress that Valluvar's ideal of the wife elsewhere (chapter 6) is a partner who safeguards the household, and that the chapter's real target is the abdication of one's own judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that a king should pursue dharma, artha and kama in balance without neglecting any, and separately advises vigilance about dangers that can arise in the royal women's quarters.
hinduism.explanation: The statecraft manual treats balance of life's aims and guarding against palace intrigue as essential to rule.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's triad of virtue, wealth and pleasure, all lost by the man who abdicates judgment, echoes Kautilya's balance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good structural parallel on the three aims; Kautilya's precautions concern security more than marital submission.

christianity.quote_or_event: God tells Adam that because he listened to his wife's voice and ate of the forbidden tree, the ground is cursed and he will toil for his bread.
christianity.explanation: In Genesis, heeding one's wife against God's command brings loss of ease and abundance.
christianity.tie_back: This is the classic biblical text behind the Kural's theme, though modern scholars and feminist theologians stress Adam's own responsibility and the shared nature of the fault.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close thematic match; its interpretation as blaming women is widely contested in modern theology.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an describes spouses as garments for one another.
islam.explanation: Husband and wife are presented as mutual protection, comfort and covering.
islam.tie_back: A counterpoint: the Qur'an's image of mutuality offers an alternative to the Kural's binary of commanding and obeying.
islam._accuracy_note: Contrasting text; included for balance rather than as a parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Rav says: Nevertheless, anyone who follows the counsel of his wife descends into Gehenna... Rav Pappa said to Abaye: But don’t people say a popular proverb: If your wife is short, stoop and whisper to her and consult with her?”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud records a harsh dictum against following a wife's counsel, immediately challenges it with a proverb urging consultation, and resolves that each applies to different spheres.
judaism.tie_back: This parallels the Kural's warning while showing a tradition debating and limiting it, which models a critical reading of the chapter.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz translation)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified with ellipsis; very close theme, and the same page also urges men to honour their wives.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Flowing in (from all objects) and watered by craving, feelings of pleasure arise in beings. Bent on pleasures and seeking enjoyment, these men fall prey to birth and decay.”
buddhism.explanation: Pleasure-seeking, watered by craving, binds beings to suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural adds that the man ruled by another's will loses even the pleasures he sought.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; general teaching on craving, not on domestic obedience.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus's allegory, the young Heracles at a crossroads is approached by two women, Vice offering easy pleasure and Virtue offering toil and lasting good, and he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The allegory frames life's direction as a choice of which voice to follow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's man who follows another's commands rather than his own judgment fails the choice Heracles made well.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles (in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Allegorical parallel; both figures are personifications, so it does not concern real wives.

philosophy.quote_or_event: John Stuart Mill argues that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself and corrupts both, and that marriage should be a partnership of equals.
philosophy.explanation: Mill's critique rejects the whole framework of command and obedience within marriage.
philosophy.tie_back: A modern counterpoint: Mill would see the Kural's problem as hierarchy itself, in either direction, rather than a husband's submission.
philosophy.source: John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Deliberately contrasting modern critique, included for scholarly balance.

kurals.tamil:
எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத் திடனுடையார்க்கு எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enserndha nenjath thitanutaiyaarkku egngnaandrum
penserndhaam pedhaimai il.
kurals.meaning: Those whose minds are given to careful thought and who have the strength and means that follow from it will never fall into the folly of being wholly ruled by attachment to a woman.
kurals.elementary: When you think things through and stay steady inside, you do not get swept away by any one wish or person. A calm, thoughtful mind keeps you in charge of your own choices.
kurals.university: En-serndha nenjam (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சம்) is 'a mind joined to deliberation'; Parimelazhagar takes it as a mind engaged in planning affairs of state, and reads idan (இடன்) not as 'firmness' (as some modern glosses do) but as 'wealth/means', citing Kural 218 ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்') and Kalittokai to establish that sense. Ytamizh's 'thitan' transliteration reflects the sandhi 'நெஞ்சத் திடன்', which modern commentators such as Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar also read as thidan (திடன், firmness of mind), so both readings circulate. Pen-serndhaam pedhaimai (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is the folly arising from attachment to the wife; Parimelazhagar says this folly is the root of all three faults treated earlier, namely desiring, fearing and obeying, so the closing verse sums up the chapter negatively. Manakkudavar explains en-serdhal as discerning the faults that arise from such attachment. Read today, the chapter's enduring core is this closing ideal of deliberative self-command, while its gendered framing belongs to its historical setting.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad compares the self to the rider of a chariot, the body to the chariot, the intellect to the charioteer, the mind to the reins and the senses to the horses.
hinduism.explanation: One whose intellect holds the reins firmly reaches the goal, while one with unruly senses does not.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's thoughtful, steady-minded person is the well-reined charioteer who is not dragged off course.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on reasoned self-command; not specific to marriage.

christianity.quote_or_event: Joseph, in Egypt, refuses the repeated advances of his master Potiphar's wife and flees, leaving his garment behind.
christianity.explanation: Joseph's steadfast integrity keeps him from yielding, at great personal cost.
christianity.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's firm-minded person who does not fall into folly.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel on firmness; the temptation is adultery rather than marital subservience.

islam.quote_or_event: Yusuf resists the governor's wife, seeking refuge in God, and later says prison is dearer to him than what he is invited to.
islam.explanation: The Qur'anic Joseph shows steadfast resolve rooted in faith.
islam.tie_back: His firmness mirrors the Kural's steady-minded person free of folly.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; parallel on firmness, not on marital deference.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city.’”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines true strength as mastery over one's own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise places real strength in a mind governed by deliberation.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified; strong match on self-mastery, without gendered framing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who delights in subduing evil thoughts, who meditates on the impurities and is ever mindful — it is he who will make an end of craving and rend asunder Mara's fetter.”
buddhism.explanation: Mindful, disciplined thought breaks the bonds of craving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's deliberative mind similarly stays free of attachment's folly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; parallel on mental discipline, with a monastic goal.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus has himself bound to the mast so he can hear the Sirens' song without steering his ship to ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Foresight lets the hero experience temptation without being ruled by it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's ideal: forethought that keeps one from folly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image of deliberation over desire; the Sirens are not wives.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Socrates likens the soul to a charioteer driving two horses, one noble and one unruly, and says the well-ordered soul is one in which reason guides the team.
philosophy.explanation: Reason must govern appetite for a soul to rise to the good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's 'mind joined to deliberation' is the charioteer in command.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on reason governing desire; not specific to marriage.
